specPoints.text: understand, in terms of the collision theory, the effect of changes in concentration, temperature, pressure and surface area on the rate of a chemical reaction

primer.text: Reactions are collision stories: particles must meet often enough, hard enough, and facing the right way. This note builds the collision trio - frequency, energy and activation hurdle - and shows how concentration, pressure, temperature and surface area each rewrite the crash statistics.

lessons.title: Successful collisions and the rate trio
lessons.opening: Reacting particles crash together constantly, yet only a few crashes make products. Collision theory splits those crashes by frequency, by energy, and by the activation hurdle, and rate ends up counting the successful collisions per unit time.
keyPoints: Rate of reaction depends on collision frequency, collision energy, and the activation energy.
Rate ultimately measures the number of successful or effective collisions per unit time.
A successful collision needs the correct orientation and sufficient energy for bonds to break and new bonds to form.
Unsuccessful collisions bounce the particles apart without reaction.

low.restatement: Particles must meet (frequency), meet hard enough (energy) and meet facing the right way (orientation) for a reaction; everything else is a bounce.
low.analogy: Darts hitting a board: you must throw often, throw hard, and aim - missing any one means no score.
low.examPointer: When asked why a condition changes rate, always end at 'more frequent successful collisions per unit time'.

medium.restatement: Only collisions that combine adequate kinetic energy with productive geometry convert reactant bonds into product bonds; the rate is a census of those effective impacts, not of all impacts.
medium.analogy: Two key-and-lock attempts per second can both fail if the key is soft or turned the wrong way; only a hard, correctly turned turn opens the lock.
medium.examPointer: Distinguish 'collision frequency' (how often) from 'successful collisions' (how often AND productive) - conflating them loses the analysis mark.

check.stem: A successful collision requires the particles to collide with

options.text: Sufficient energy and the correct orientation
options.explanation: Both conditions together let bonds break and new bonds form.

options.text: High speed only, whatever the direction
options.explanation: Energy without orientation leaves the collision ineffective.

options.text: Correct orientation only, whatever the energy
options.explanation: Orientation without the activation energy still bounces the pair apart.

options.text: Identical masses in each collision
options.explanation: Particle masses need not match for reaction.

check.stem: An unsuccessful collision is one in which the particles

options.text: Bounce apart because of wrong orientation or too little energy
options.explanation: Both failure routes leave the reactants unchanged.

options.text: Always combine to form a temporary compound
options.explanation: No product forms in an unsuccessful collision.

options.text: Transfer all their energy to the surroundings
options.explanation: Energy transfer is not the definition of failure here.

options.text: Stick together as an intermediate
options.explanation: Unsuccessful collisions separate the particles again.

check.stem: The rate of a chemical reaction is ultimately determined by

options.text: The number of successful collisions per unit time
options.explanation: Rate counts effective collisions, not raw collision numbers.

options.text: The total number of collisions however weak
options.explanation: Most collisions fail; counting them overstates the rate.

options.text: The mass of the largest reactant particle
options.explanation: Mass is not the direct determinant.

options.text: The temperature alone in every case
options.explanation: Temperature matters, but only through the collision factors it feeds.

check.stem: Which list gives the three rate-controlling factors named in collision theory?

options.text: Collision frequency, collision energy, activation energy
options.explanation: These three together decide how many collisions succeed.

options.text: Pressure, catalysts and light intensity
options.explanation: These are condition levers, not the theory's named trio.

options.text: Molar mass, density and polarity
options.explanation: None of these is the collision-theory trio.

options.text: Surface area, temperature and a colour change
options.explanation: The colour change is a measuring method, not a factor.

check.stem: Bonds in the reactants break and new bonds form only when

options.text: A collision carries at least the activation energy and correct geometry
options.explanation: The energy hurdle and orientation together allow bond reorganisation.

options.text: Any collision occurs, however gentle
options.explanation: Gentle collisions bounce off without reaction.

options.text: The particles are at absolute rest
options.explanation: Resting particles do not collide at all.

options.text: A catalyst is always present
options.explanation: Catalysts help but uncatalysed successful collisions still occur.

check.stem: State the two conditions for an effective collision.
check.modelAnswer: The particles must collide with energy at least equal to the activation energy and in the correct orientation.

check.stem: Define an unsuccessful collision.
check.modelAnswer: A collision in which the particles lack the energy or the orientation needed to react, so they bounce apart without forming products.

check.stem: Explain why most collisions do not lead to reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Most colliding pairs either lack the minimum activation energy or meet in an unproductive orientation, so bonds stay intact and the particles separate unchanged.

check.stem: A reaction between two gases suddenly speeds up when the mixture is compressed. Explain using collision theory.
check.modelAnswer: Compression packs the same particles into a smaller volume, raising collision frequency; with the same fraction of successful collisions, more effective collisions occur per unit time and the rate rises.

lessons.title: Controlling collision frequency
lessons.opening: Four levers move collision frequency: concentration, pressure, temperature and particle size. But frequency alone is not the whole story - each collision must also carry enough energy, which is where most pairs fail.
keyPoints: Collision frequency counts the collisions between reactant particles in each unit of time.
Raising concentration, pressure, temperature or surface area all raise collision frequency.
Higher concentration or pressure packs more particles into the same space for more frequent meetings.
Not every collision succeeds: most pairs lack the energy to break the necessary bonds.

low.restatement: More particles in less space, faster-moving particles, or more exposed surface all raise the meeting rate; but only collisions with sufficient energy can react.
low.analogy: A busy crossroads: more traffic means more encounters, yet only encounters with enough momentum to unlock the gate lead anywhere.
low.examPointer: Pair each condition with its mechanism: concentration/pressure = more particles per volume; temperature = more kinetic energy; surface area = more exposed particles.

medium.restatement: Frequency is a counting problem - collisions per second - while success is an energy problem per collision. Temperature is the one lever that raises both counts at once: more collisions and a bigger energetic share of them.
medium.analogy: Speeding up a queue raises the number of handshakes per minute, but only firm grips (energetic collisions) conclude deals.
medium.examPointer: Do not claim higher concentration raises collision energy - it only raises collision frequency.

check.stem: Increasing the concentration of a solution increases rate because

options.text: More particles occupy the same volume, so collisions happen more often
options.explanation: Crowding raises collision frequency, hence more successful collisions per unit time.

options.text: Each collision carries more energy
options.explanation: Concentration does not change the energy of individual collisions.

options.text: The activation energy becomes smaller
options.explanation: Ea is fixed for a given reaction at a given temperature.

options.text: The particles change orientation more efficiently
options.explanation: Orientation is unaffected by concentration.

check.stem: Raising the pressure of a gas reaction raises rate because

options.text: The same number of particles now sits in a smaller volume, colliding more often
options.explanation: Compression concentrates the particles, lifting collision frequency.

options.text: The molecules gain kinetic energy from compression
options.explanation: Kinetic energy rises with temperature, not with pressure at fixed T.

options.text: The activation energy barrier drops
options.explanation: The barrier is a property of the reaction, not the pressure.

options.text: Fewer particles are needed for the reaction
options.explanation: Stoichiometry is unchanged by pressure.

check.stem: Which condition raises BOTH collision frequency and collision energy?

options.text: Increasing the temperature
options.explanation: Heat raises kinetic energy, speeding particles so they meet more often and hit harder.

options.text: Increasing the concentration
options.explanation: Concentration raises frequency only.

options.text: Grinding a solid into powder
options.explanation: Surface area raises frequency only.

options.text: Adding an inert gas at constant volume
options.explanation: Inert gas barely changes the reactant collision count.

check.stem: Increasing the surface area of a solid reactant works by

options.text: Exposing more particles for collision at the interface
options.explanation: More available surface means more collision opportunities per unit time.

options.text: Lowering the activation energy of the reaction
options.explanation: Ea is unchanged by subdivision.

options.text: Increasing the energy of each collision
options.explanation: Collision energy is set by temperature, not surface area.

options.text: Dissolving the solid faster
options.explanation: Dissolution is not the mechanism for a solid-solid or solid-gas reaction.

check.stem: A mixture has frequent collisions yet reacts slowly. The best explanation is

options.text: Most collisions lack sufficient energy to overcome the activation energy
options.explanation: High frequency with low success still gives a slow rate.

options.text: The collisions are too frequent to succeed
options.explanation: There is no such effect; frequency helps.

options.text: The particles are colliding in the wrong container
options.explanation: Container choice is not a collision-theory factor.

options.text: The activation energy is zero
options.explanation: With zero Ea almost every energetic collision would succeed.

check.stem: State four ways to increase collision frequency.
check.modelAnswer: Increase concentration, increase pressure, increase temperature, or increase the surface area of the reacting particles.

check.stem: Define collision frequency.
check.modelAnswer: The number of collisions between reactant particles per unit time in the system.

check.stem: Explain why temperature is the most powerful of the four frequency levers.
check.modelAnswer: Temperature raises collision frequency and also increases the proportion of collisions carrying at least the activation energy, so it lifts both factors that decide the rate.

check.stem: Marble chips react faster as powder than as lumps with the same acid. Explain with collision theory, and state one lever the student must keep constant for a fair test.
check.modelAnswer: Powder exposes far more surface, so more acid particles collide with exposed solid per unit time, raising successful collisions; concentration and temperature must be kept constant for the comparison to be fair.

lessons.title: Activation energy and reaction profiles
lessons.opening: Every reaction charges a toll: the activation energy, the minimum energy a collision must carry before bonds will reorganise. Exothermic profiles show a low hill; endothermic ones a taller climb, because reactants start below their products.
keyPoints: The activation energy Ea is the minimum energy reactant particles need before reaction can occur.
Exothermic reactants start above their products, leaving a relatively small barrier to climb.
Endothermic reactants start below their products, so the barrier to climb is relatively larger.
Even correctly oriented collisions fail if their energy is below Ea.

low.restatement: The energy hill between reactants and products is the activation energy; exothermic reactants sit high and pay a small toll, endothermic reactants sit low and pay a larger one.
low.analogy: A summit between two valleys: walking downhill-to-downhill is an easy climb; climbing from a low valley to a high one is a longer haul.
low.examPointer: On profiles, always mark Ea as the vertical gap from reactants to the curve's peak, and label the exothermic/endothermic starting levels.

medium.restatement: Kinetic energy distributions explain the toll: only the tail of particles beyond Ea can react regardless of orientation. Endothermic reactions pay the toll plus the net energy gain, which is why their Ea is comparatively larger.
medium.analogy: A theme-park ride with a height bar: only riders taller than the bar (energy above Ea) get through, however perfectly they queue (orientation).
medium.examPointer: Quote 'minimum energy' verbatim in Ea definitions and connect relative profile heights to exothermic versus endothermic classification.

check.stem: Activation energy is

options.text: The minimum energy colliding particles must possess for a reaction to occur
options.explanation: Below Ea, no collision can convert reactants into products.

options.text: The total energy released by an exothermic reaction
options.explanation: That is the enthalpy change, not Ea.

options.text: The energy of the products minus the reactants
options.explanation: That describes ΔH, not the barrier height.

options.text: The average kinetic energy of the mixture
options.explanation: The average sits below Ea for most reactions; Ea is the threshold.

check.stem: On an energy profile for an endothermic reaction, the reactants sit

options.text: Lower than the products, giving a relatively larger activation energy
options.explanation: Climbing uphill needs a bigger barrier, matching endothermic absorption.

options.text: Higher than the products, giving a small barrier
options.explanation: That describes the exothermic profile.

options.text: At the same level as the products
options.explanation: Endothermic reactions have a net energy rise.

options.text: At the curve's maximum
options.explanation: The maximum is the transition state, not the reactants.

check.stem: A collision with perfect orientation still fails when

options.text: Its energy is below the activation energy
options.explanation: Both conditions are required; failing one is enough to bounce the pair apart.

options.text: The particles are gases
options.explanation: Gas-phase collisions succeed regularly when conditions are met.

options.text: The temperature is high
options.explanation: High temperature raises success, not failure.

options.text: A catalyst is absent
options.explanation: Catalysis is optional; uncatalysed successful collisions occur.

check.stem: Why is the exothermic barrier comparatively small?

options.text: The reactants already sit higher in energy than the products
options.explanation: Starting high means less climb to the transition state.

options.text: Exothermic reactions release no energy
options.explanation: They release the surplus after the barrier is crossed.

options.text: Their particles always collide harder
options.explanation: Collision energy depends on temperature, not reaction type.

options.text: Products in exothermic reactions have no energy
options.explanation: Products still carry energy; they are simply lower than reactants.

check.stem: Rate experiments commonly measure reaction progress by tracking

options.text: Reactant lost, product formed, a colour change, or precipitate formation timing
options.explanation: All four translate successful collisions into observable change.

options.text: Only the mass of the catalyst
options.explanation: Catalyst mass is constant and uninformative here.

options.text: The activation energy directly
options.explanation: Ea is deduced from analysis, not read during the run.

options.text: The particle orientation with a camera
options.explanation: Orientation is a model concept, not a lab measurement.

check.stem: Define activation energy.
check.modelAnswer: The minimum energy that reactant particles must possess for a collision to lead to reaction.

check.stem: Compare the activation energy of exothermic and endothermic reactions.
check.modelAnswer: Exothermic reactions have a relatively small Ea because reactants start above products; endothermic reactions have a relatively larger Ea because reactants start below products.

check.stem: Explain why a catalyst lowers Ea without changing collision frequency.
check.modelAnswer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower energy barrier, so the same collision population now has a larger fraction above the reduced Ea - frequency is untouched, success fraction rises.

check.stem: Two reactions share identical conditions and collision frequencies, but reaction A is much faster. Sketch reasoning in words comparing their Ea values.
check.modelAnswer: Reaction A must have the lower activation energy: with equal collision counts, the mixture whose energy distribution clears the smaller barrier yields far more successful collisions per unit time.

glossary.definition: The number of collisions between reactant particles per unit time in the system.
A collision with the correct orientation and at least the activation energy, producing reaction.
The minimum energy a collision must carry before reactant bonds can break and products form.

figures.caption: (a) shows an ineffective collision due to the particles not having enough energy whereas (b) shows an effective collision where the particles have the correct orientation and enough energy for a chemical reaction to take place
The diagram shows that the reactants are higher in energy than the products in the exothermic reaction, so the energy needed for the reactants to go over the energy barrier is relatively small
The diagram shows that the reactants are lower in energy than the products in the endothermic reaction, so the energy needed for the reactants to go over the energy barrier is relatively large
